summary: Advises that the ip6.int domain is deprecated for standards-conformant IPv6 implementations. It is a best current practice document about which domain to use for reverse lookups of IPv6 addresses.

eli5.summary: An old street name has been replaced on the map. This memo tells everyone to stop using the old name for IPv6 reverse lookups.

subtitle: Switch from ip6.int to ip6.arpa for IPv6 reverse DNS lookups

tldr.problem: IPv6 implementations had been using the ip6.int domain for reverse DNS lookups (finding a domain name from an IP address), but this was deprecated in 2001 in favor of ip6.arpa to align with proper DNS infrastructure standards.
tldr.mechanism: This BCP document formally completes the transition by declaring that as of September 1, 2005, all standards-conformant IPv6 implementations must use ip6.arpa for reverse mapping instead of ip6.int.
tldr.outcome: The ip6.int domain was deprecated, and IPv6 implementations now exclusively use ip6.arpa for reverse DNS lookups, following the same pattern as IPv4's in-addr.arpa domain.

today: RFC 4159 set the formal deadline for the deprecation. IPv6 implementations have used ip6.arpa exclusively for reverse DNS lookups since 2005, and ip6.int is no longer part of IPv6 standards.

sections.title: The IPv6 Standards Change
sections.content:
When IPv6 addresses first needed to be mapped back to domain names through the Domain Name System, the IETF initially used the ip6.int domain for this purpose. In August 2001, RFC 3152 recommended deprecating ip6.int in favor of ip6.arpa, following the pattern already established for IPv4 reverse lookups, which use in-addr.arpa.

This RFC formally completes that transition. As of September 1, 2005, standards-conformant IPv6 implementations must use ip6.arpa and are no longer permitted to use ip6.int for reverse DNS lookups.
sections.eli5: When computers look up what website an address belongs to, they used to ask about a place called ip6.int. Now they should ask about ip6.arpa instead, which is better organized.

sections.title: New Domain Requirements
sections.content:
Reverse DNS for IPv6 addresses works by taking the address and converting it into a DNS query. For example, an IPv6 address is written in reverse order, hex digit by hex digit, and appended to the domain name. Under the old standard, this query was made against ip6.int. The new standard directs all such queries to ip6.arpa instead.

The Regional Internet Registries (RIRs), which manage IP address assignments, were directed to stop maintaining the ip6.int zone and transition their infrastructure to support ip6.arpa for IPv6 reverse lookups.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking a directory called ip6.int for an address lookup, you now ask ip6.arpa. It is the same kind of question, just sent to a different directory.

sections.title: Security and Compatibility
sections.content:
The change from ip6.int to ip6.arpa creates no new security threats. While DNS spoofing of address-to-name mappings has been exploited in IPv4, the removal of ip6.int from the standard specification simply closes one old path and directs users to the newer, standardized one.

This alignment with IPv4's approach (which already used the .arpa domain) makes IPv6 reverse DNS more consistent with existing Internet infrastructure and standards practices.
sections.eli5: Switching to a new directory does not make things less safe. Everyone now looks in one place (ip6.arpa) instead of some old place (ip6.int), making things simpler and more organized.

references.text: Bush, R., "Delegation of IP6.ARPA", BCP 49, RFC 3152, August 2001.
